verses.text: This happened in the days of King Ahasuerus, who ruled over a hundred twenty-seven provinces from India to Ethiopia.
At that time King Ahasuerus ruled from his royal throne at the palace in Susa.
In the third year of his reign, he gave a banquet for all his officials and servants, with the military leaders of Persia and Media, the nobles, and the provincial leaders in attendance.
For a hundred eighty days he showed off the wealth of his glorious kingdom and the splendor of his royal power.
When that was over, the king gave a seven-day banquet in the garden courtyard of his palace for everyone in the fortress of Susa, from the least to the greatest.
White and blue curtains hung from silver rings on marble columns, tied with cords of fine linen and purple cloth. Gold and silver couches stood on a pavement of red, white, yellow, and black marble.
Drinks were served in gold cups of many designs, and there was plenty of royal wine because the king gave it freely.
By royal order no one was required to drink. The king had told all his palace officials to give each guest as much or as little as he wanted.
Queen Vashti also gave a banquet for the women inside King Ahasuerus's palace.
On the seventh day, when the king was cheerful from drinking wine, he gave an order to the seven eunuchs who served him: Mehuman, Biztha, Harbona, Bigtha, Abagtha, Zethar, and Carcass.
He told them to bring Queen Vashti before him wearing her royal crown so he could show the people and officials how beautiful she was.
Queen Vashti refused to come when the eunuchs brought the king's order. The king was furious, and his anger burned within him.
The king consulted the wise men who understood the times. It was his custom to ask those who knew the law and how to apply it.

His closest advisers were Carshena, Shethar, Admatha, Tarshish, Meres, Marsena, and Memucan, seven leaders of Persia and Media who had direct access to the king and held the highest positions in the kingdom.
"Under the law, what should we do to Queen Vashti for refusing to obey the order King Ahasuerus sent through the eunuchs?"
Memucan answered before the king and the officials, "Queen Vashti has wronged the king, all his officials, and the people in every province of King Ahasuerus.
Women everywhere will hear what the queen did and look down on their husbands. They'll say, 'King Ahasuerus ordered Queen Vashti to appear before him, and she refused to come.'
Today the noblewomen of Persia and Media who hear what the queen did will speak the same way to the king's officials. There'll be no end to the disrespect and anger.

If it pleases the king, let him issue a royal decree and have it written into the laws of Persia and Media so it can't be changed. Vashti must never come before King Ahasuerus again, and the king should give her position as queen to someone better than she is.
When the king's decree is announced throughout his vast kingdom, all wives will honor their husbands, whatever their rank."
The king and his officials liked this advice, so the king did what Memucan had proposed.

He sent letters to every province of his kingdom, in each province's script and every people's language, ordering that every man should rule his own household and speak the language of his own people.
After King Ahasuerus's anger cooled, he thought about Vashti, what she had done, and the decree he'd issued against her.
The king's attendants said, "Let a search be made for beautiful young women who have never been with a man.

Appoint officers in every province to gather those young women at the fortress of Susa. Let them stay in the women's quarters under Hegai, the king's eunuch in charge of the women, and give them beauty treatments.
Then let the young woman who pleases the king become queen in Vashti's place." The king liked the idea and acted on it.
A Jewish man named Mordecai lived in the fortress of Susa. He was the son of Jair, descended from Shimei and Kish, a Benjamite.
His family had been taken from Jerusalem among the exiles deported with King Jeconiah of Judah by King Nebuchadnezzar of Babylon.

Mordecai had raised his cousin Hadassah, also called Esther, because she had no father or mother. She was lovely in form and appearance. When her parents died, Mordecai took her in as his own daughter.
When the king's order was announced, many young women were brought to the fortress of Susa and placed in Hegai's care. Esther was brought into the palace and placed in his care as well.

Hegai liked Esther and treated her kindly. He promptly gave her beauty treatments and her share of food, assigned her seven attendants chosen from the palace, and moved them all to the best part of the women's quarters.
Esther hadn't told anyone who her people or her relatives were, because Mordecai had told her to keep it to herself.
Every day Mordecai walked in front of the courtyard of the women's quarters to find out how Esther was doing and what would happen to her.
Each woman's turn to go to King Ahasuerus came after twelve months of beauty treatments: six months with oil of myrrh and six months with perfumes and cosmetics.
When a young woman went to the king, she could take whatever she wanted from the women's quarters to the royal residence.

She went in the evening and returned the next morning to the second women's quarters, under Shaashgaz, the king's eunuch in charge of the concubines. She could only see the king again if he was pleased with her and called for her by name.

When it was Esther's turn, she asked only for what Hegai, the king's eunuch in charge of the women, recommended. Esther was the daughter of Abihail, Mordecai's uncle, and Mordecai had adopted her. Everyone who saw her looked on her favorably.
Esther was taken to King Ahasuerus in his royal residence in the tenth month, Tebeth, in the seventh year of his reign.

The king loved Esther more than any of the other women and showed her more favor and kindness than any of the other young women. He put the royal crown on her head and made her queen in Vashti's place.
Then the king held a great banquet for his officials and servants in Esther's honor. He declared a holiday throughout the provinces and gave gifts with royal generosity.
When the young women were gathered a second time, Mordecai was sitting at the king's gate.
Esther still hadn't disclosed her family or her people. She followed Mordecai's instructions, just as she had when he was raising her.
While Mordecai was sitting at the king's gate, two of the king's eunuchs who guarded the entrance, Bigthan and Teresh, became angry and plotted to kill King Ahasuerus.
Mordecai found out about the plot and told Queen Esther. She told the king and gave Mordecai credit for the report.
The matter was investigated and found to be true. Both men were hanged, and the event was recorded in the royal chronicles in the king's presence.
After these events King Ahasuerus promoted Haman son of Hammedatha the Agagite and gave him a position above all the other officials.
Everyone serving the king at the palace gate bowed and paid Haman honor, as the king had ordered. Mordecai refused to bow or pay him honor.
The royal servants at the gate asked Mordecai, "Why are you disobeying the king's order?"
They spoke to him day after day, but he wouldn't listen. So they told Haman to find out whether Mordecai's explanation would be accepted. He had told them he was Jewish.
When Haman saw that Mordecai wouldn't bow to him or honor him, he became furious.

When Haman learned who Mordecai's people were, he decided that going after Mordecai alone wasn't enough. He looked for a way to destroy all the Jews, Mordecai's people, throughout the kingdom of Ahasuerus.
In the first month, Nisan, of the twelfth year of King Ahasuerus, they cast the Pur, meaning the lot, in Haman's presence to choose a day and a month. The choice fell on the twelfth month, Adar.

Haman told King Ahasuerus, "There is a people scattered among the peoples in every province of your kingdom. Their laws differ from everyone else's, and they disobey the king's laws. It isn't in your interest to let them remain.
If it pleases the king, issue a decree to destroy them. I'll pay ten thousand talents of silver to the officials in charge of the king's business to put into the royal treasuries."
The king took off his signet ring and gave it to Haman son of Hammedatha the Agagite, the enemy of the Jews.
The king told Haman, "The silver is yours, and so are the people. Do with them as you see fit."

On the thirteenth day of the first month, the king's scribes wrote down everything Haman ordered for the royal governors, provincial rulers, and leaders of every people, using each province's script and each people's language. They wrote in King Ahasuerus's name and sealed the decree with his ring.

Couriers carried the letters to every province. They ordered the killing of all Jews, young and old, women and children, on one day, the thirteenth day of the twelfth month, Adar. They also authorized the seizure of their possessions.
A copy of the decree was published throughout every province and made known to all the peoples so they could be ready for that day.
The couriers went out quickly at the king's command, and the decree was announced in the fortress of Susa. The king and Haman sat down to drink, while the city of Susa was in confusion.
When Mordecai learned everything that had happened, he tore his clothes, put on sackcloth and ashes, and went into the middle of the city, crying out loudly and bitterly.
He went as far as the king's gate, because no one wearing sackcloth was allowed inside.
In every province the king's decree reached, the Jews mourned deeply. They fasted, wept, and cried out, and many lay in sackcloth and ashes.
When Esther's attendants and eunuchs told her what was happening, she was deeply distressed. She sent clothes for Mordecai to wear instead of sackcloth, but he refused them.
Esther called Hathach, one of the king's eunuchs assigned to serve her. She ordered him to ask Mordecai what was happening and why.
Hathach went to Mordecai in the city square in front of the king's gate.
Mordecai told him everything that had happened and the exact amount Haman had promised to pay into the royal treasuries for the destruction of the Jews.
He gave Hathach a copy of the decree issued in Susa to destroy the Jews. He told him to show it to Esther, explain it, and urge her to go to the king and plead for her people.
Hathach returned and told Esther what Mordecai had said.
Esther gave Hathach this message for Mordecai:

"All the king's officials and everyone in the provinces know the law. Anyone, man or woman, who goes into the inner court to see the king without being summoned must die, unless the king holds out the gold scepter and spares them. I haven't been summoned to the king for thirty days."
Esther's words were reported to Mordecai.
Mordecai sent back this reply: "Don't assume that living in the king's palace will let you escape when the rest of the Jews are in danger.
If you stay silent now, relief and rescue will come to the Jews from somewhere else, but you and your family will die. Who knows whether you became queen for a time like this?"
Then Esther sent Mordecai this reply:

"Go gather all the Jews in Susa and fast for me. Go without food and drink for three days, night and day. My attendants and I will fast too. Then I'll go to the king, even though it's against the law. If I die, I die."
Mordecai went and did everything Esther had asked him to do.
On the third day Esther put on her royal robes and stood in the inner courtyard of the palace, across from the king's hall. The king was sitting on his throne inside the hall, facing the entrance.
When the king saw Queen Esther standing in the courtyard, he welcomed her by holding out the gold scepter in his hand. Esther stepped forward and touched its tip.
The king asked, "What is it, Queen Esther? What's your request? I'll give you even half the kingdom."
Esther answered, "If it pleases the king, I'd like you and Haman to come today to a banquet I've prepared for you."
The king said, "Bring Haman quickly so we can do what Esther has asked." So the king and Haman went to the banquet Esther had prepared.
While they were drinking wine, the king said to Esther, "What do you ask? You'll have it. What would you like me to do? I'll do it, even if you ask for half the kingdom."
Esther answered, "Here is what I ask.
If I've found favor with the king and it pleases him to grant my request, let the king and Haman come to the banquet I'll prepare for them tomorrow. Then I'll answer the king's question."
Haman left that day in high spirits. But when he saw Mordecai at the king's gate and Mordecai stayed seated and didn't move for him, Haman was furious.
He held himself back and went home. Then he sent for his friends and his wife Zeresh.
Haman bragged to them about his wealth, his many children, every promotion the king had given him, and how the king had raised him above the other officials and servants.
He added, "Queen Esther invited only me to join the king at her banquet, and tomorrow she's invited me back with the king.
Yet none of this gives me any satisfaction as long as I see Mordecai the Jew sitting at the king's gate."

His wife Zeresh and all his friends said, "Have a gallows built fifty cubits high. In the morning ask the king to hang Mordecai on it. Then you can go to the banquet with the king in good spirits." The idea pleased Haman, and he had the gallows built.
That night the king couldn't sleep. He ordered the royal chronicles brought in and read aloud to him.
The records showed that Mordecai had reported Bigthana and Teresh, two of the king's eunuchs who guarded the entrance and had plotted against King Ahasuerus.
The king asked, "What honor or recognition did Mordecai receive for this?" His attendants replied, "Nothing was done for him."
The king asked, "Who's in the courtyard?" Haman had just come into the outer court of the palace to ask the king to hang Mordecai on the gallows he'd prepared for him.
The king's attendants answered, "Haman is in the courtyard." The king said, "Let him in."
When Haman came in, the king asked him, "What should be done for the man the king wants to honor?" Haman thought, "Who would the king want to honor more than me?"
He answered the king, "For the man the king wants to honor,
bring out a robe the king himself has worn and a horse the king rides, with a royal crown on its head.

Put the robe and horse in the care of one of the king's highest officials. Have him dress the man the king wants to honor and lead him on horseback through the city square, announcing, 'This is what happens to the man the king wants to honor!'"
The king told Haman, "Hurry. Take the robe and horse, just as you said, and do this for Mordecai the Jew, who sits at the king's gate. Carry out everything you've suggested."
So Haman took the robe and horse, dressed Mordecai, and led him on horseback through the city square. He announced in front of him, "This is what happens to the man the king wants to honor!"
Mordecai went back to the king's gate. Haman hurried home in mourning with his head covered.

Haman told his wife Zeresh and all his friends what had happened. His advisers and Zeresh told him, "If Mordecai is Jewish and you've already begun to fall before him, you won't get the better of him. You're sure to fall before him."
While they were still talking, the king's eunuchs arrived and hurried Haman to Esther's banquet.
The king and Haman came to the banquet with Queen Esther.

On the second day, as they drank wine, the king asked Esther again, "What are you asking for, Queen Esther? I'll grant it. What would you like me to do? I'll do it, even if you ask for half the kingdom."
Queen Esther answered, "If I've found favor with you, Your Majesty, and if it pleases you, spare my life. That's what I'm asking. And spare my people. That's my request.

My people and I have been sold to be destroyed, killed, and wiped out. If we'd only been sold as male and female slaves, I would have kept quiet, though our enemy couldn't have made up for the king's loss."
King Ahasuerus asked Queen Esther, "Who is he? Where is the man who dared to do this?"
Esther said, "Our enemy is right here. It's this wicked Haman!" Haman was terrified in front of the king and queen.
The king got up from the banquet in a rage and went into the palace garden. Haman stood to beg Queen Esther for his life, because he could see the king had decided to punish him.

When the king returned from the garden to the banquet room, Haman had fallen onto the couch where Esther was. The king said, "Will he even assault the queen here in my own palace, right in front of me?" As soon as the king spoke, the attendants covered Haman's face.

Harbonah, one of the eunuchs serving the king, said, "There's a gallows fifty cubits high at Haman's house. He built it for Mordecai, the man who spoke up to save the king." The king said, "Hang him on it."
So they hanged Haman on the gallows he'd prepared for Mordecai. Then the king's anger subsided.
That day King Ahasuerus gave Queen Esther the estate of Haman, the enemy of the Jews. Mordecai came before the king because Esther had told him how they were related.
The king took off the signet ring he'd taken back from Haman and gave it to Mordecai. Esther put Mordecai in charge of Haman's estate.
Esther spoke to the king again. She fell at his feet and begged him through tears to stop the harm Haman the Agagite had plotted against the Jews.
The king held out the gold scepter to Esther, so she got up and stood before him.

She said, "If it pleases the king, if I've found favor with him, and if this seems right to him and he is pleased with me, let an order be written reversing the letters Haman son of Hammedatha the Agagite wrote to destroy the Jews in all the royal provinces.
How can I bear to see disaster come upon my people? How can I bear to watch my own family be destroyed?"
King Ahasuerus told Queen Esther and Mordecai the Jew, "I've given Esther Haman's estate, and he was hanged because he attacked the Jews.
Write whatever you think best for the Jews in the king's name and seal it with the king's ring. No one can revoke a document written in the king's name and sealed with his ring."

The royal scribes were called on the twenty-third day of the third month, Sivan. They wrote everything Mordecai ordered for the Jews and for the governors and officials of the hundred twenty-seven provinces from India to Ethiopia. They used each province's script and each people's language, including the script and language of the Jews.
Mordecai wrote in King Ahasuerus's name and sealed the letters with the king's ring. He sent them out with couriers riding fast horses bred for royal service.

The letters granted the Jews in every city the right to gather and defend their lives. They could destroy any armed force from any people or province that attacked them, their children, or their women, and take their attackers' possessions.
This permission was for one day throughout King Ahasuerus's provinces, the thirteenth day of the twelfth month, Adar.
A copy of the order was made public to all peoples in each province so the Jews could be ready that day to take vengeance on their enemies.
At the king's urgent command, the couriers rode out quickly on royal horses. The decree was also announced in the fortress of Susa.
Mordecai left the king's presence wearing blue and white royal robes, a large gold crown, and a robe of fine linen and purple cloth. The city of Susa shouted with joy.
For the Jews there was light, gladness, joy, and honor.
In every province and city where the king's decree arrived, the Jews celebrated with joy, feasting, and a holiday. Many people of the land became Jews because fear of the Jews had come over them.

On the thirteenth day of the twelfth month, Adar, the king's orders were due to take effect. The enemies of the Jews had hoped to overpower them that day, but things were reversed. The Jews overcame those who hated them.

The Jews gathered in their cities throughout King Ahasuerus's provinces to defend themselves against anyone who meant to harm them. No one could stand against them because the people had become afraid of them.
The provincial leaders, local governors, and royal officials all helped the Jews because they were afraid of Mordecai.
Mordecai held a powerful position in the palace, and word about him spread through every province. He was growing more powerful all the time.
The Jews struck down their enemies with the sword, killing and destroying them. They did as they wished with those who hated them.
In the fortress of Susa, the Jews killed five hundred men.
They killed Parshandatha, Dalphon, and Aspatha,
Poratha, Adalia, and Aridatha,
Parmashta, Arisai, Aridai, and Vaizatha,
the ten sons of Haman son of Hammedatha, the enemy of the Jews. They took none of their property.
The number of people killed in the fortress of Susa was reported to the king that day.

The king told Queen Esther, "The Jews have killed five hundred men in the fortress of Susa, including Haman's ten sons. What must they have done in the rest of the provinces? Now what else are you asking for? I'll grant it. What more do you request? It will be done."
Esther answered, "If it pleases the king, allow the Jews in Susa to act under today's decree tomorrow too, and have the bodies of Haman's ten sons hung on the gallows."
The king gave the order. A decree was issued in Susa, and Haman's ten sons were hung.
The Jews in Susa gathered again on the fourteenth day of Adar and killed three hundred men there, but took none of their property.

The other Jews across the king's provinces gathered to defend themselves and found relief from their enemies. They killed seventy-five thousand of those who hated them, but took none of their property.
This happened on the thirteenth day of Adar. On the fourteenth they rested and made it a day of feasting and joy.
The Jews in Susa gathered on the thirteenth and fourteenth days, then rested on the fifteenth and made it a day of feasting and joy.
That's why Jews who live in villages and unwalled towns celebrate the fourteenth day of Adar as a holiday, feasting, rejoicing, and sending gifts of food to one another.
Mordecai wrote down what had happened and sent letters to the Jews in all the provinces of King Ahasuerus, near and far.
He told them to observe the fourteenth and fifteenth days of Adar every year,

because these were the days when the Jews found relief from their enemies. That month their sorrow turned into joy and their mourning into a holiday. They were to mark those days by feasting and celebrating, sending food to one another, and giving gifts to people in need.
The Jews agreed to continue the custom they had begun, just as Mordecai had written to them.
Haman son of Hammedatha the Agagite, the enemy of all the Jews, had plotted to destroy them and had cast the Pur, meaning the lot, to decide when to wipe them out.
When the king learned of it, he issued a written order that Haman's evil plot against the Jews should fall back on his own head and that he and his sons should be hung on the gallows.
That's why the days are called Purim, from the word Pur. In light of the letter, what they had seen, and what had happened to them,
the Jews took on a lasting obligation for themselves, their descendants, and everyone who joined them. They would observe these two days each year in the way prescribed and at the appointed time.

These days were to be remembered and observed from generation to generation in every family, province, and city. The Jews were to keep celebrating Purim, and their descendants were never to forget it.
Queen Esther daughter of Abihail and Mordecai the Jew wrote with full authority to confirm this second letter about Purim.
Mordecai sent letters with words of peace and truth to all the Jews in the hundred twenty-seven provinces of Ahasuerus's kingdom.

The letters confirmed the appointed dates for Purim, as Mordecai the Jew and Queen Esther had decreed and as the people had pledged for themselves and their descendants, along with the observances of fasting and mourning.
Esther's command confirmed these practices for Purim, and it was written in the book.
King Ahasuerus imposed a tax on the mainland and the islands of the sea.
The full record of his powerful deeds and of the high position he gave Mordecai is written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Media and Persia.

Mordecai the Jew was second only to King Ahasuerus. He was highly respected among the Jews and well regarded by many of his fellow Jews, because he worked for their welfare and spoke for the peace of all their descendants.
